pr_body:
This is based on top of #47248.  I will rebase whenever / however that PR is resolved.

---

This adds a `config/Dockerfile.erb` template file that will be rendered to `Dockerfile` when an app is created, and a `bin/rails docker:render` command to re-render the file on demand.

The template file uses helpers defined in a publicly documented `DockerfileHelpers` module:
   
  ```erb
  <%#
  Run `bin/rails docker:render` to render this template to a Dockerfile in your
  application's root directory. For more information about the helpers used in
  this template, see https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/Rails/DockerfileHelpers.html
  -%>

  # Base stage for build and final stages.
  FROM ruby:<%= ruby_version %>-slim as base

  WORKDIR /rails
  RUN useradd rails

  ENV RAILS_ENV=<%= Rails.env %>

  <%= install_packages runtime_packages, skip_recommends: true %>
   

  # Throw-away build stage to reduce the size of final image.
  FROM base as build

  <%= install_packages buildtime_packages %>

  COPY Gemfile Gemfile.lock* .
  <%= install_gems %>

  COPY . .
  <%= prepare_app %>

  RUN mkdir /artifacts && cp -r --parents $PWD /usr/local/bundle /artifacts
   

  # Final stage for application image.
  FROM base

  COPY --from=build --chown=1000 /artifacts /

  USER 1000
  ENTRYPOINT ["bin/docker-entrypoint"]
  CMD ["bin/rails", "server"]
  EXPOSE 3000
  ```

Which results in a `Dockerfile` like:

  ```dockerfile
  # syntax = docker/dockerfile:1

  ########################################################################
  # This file was rendered from `config/Dockerfile.erb`.
  #
  # Instead of editing this file, edit `config/Dockerfile.erb`, then run
  # `bin/rails docker:render`.
  ########################################################################

  # Base stage for build and final stages.
  FROM ruby:3.1.2-slim as base

  WORKDIR /rails
  RUN useradd rails

  ENV RAILS_ENV=production

  RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
      --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt,sharing=locked \
      apt-get update -qq && \
      apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y libsqlite3-0
   

  # Throw-away build stage to reduce the size of final image.
  FROM base as build

  RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
      --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt,sharing=locked \
      apt-get update -qq && \
      apt-get install -y build-essential git libsqlite3-0

  COPY Gemfile Gemfile.lock* .
  RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/usr/local/bundle/cache,sharing=locked \
      gem update --system --no-document && \
      bundle config set --local without "development" && \
      bundle install && \
      bundle exec bootsnap precompile --gemfile

  COPY . .
  RUN --mount=type=cache,target=tmp/cache/assets \
      bundle exec bootsnap precompile app/ lib/ && \
      SECRET_KEY_BASE_DUMMY=1 bin/rails assets:precompile

  RUN mkdir /artifacts && cp -r --parents $PWD /usr/local/bundle /artifacts
   

  # Final stage for application image.
  FROM base

  COPY --from=build --chown=1000 /artifacts /

  USER 1000
  ENTRYPOINT ["bin/docker-entrypoint"]
  CMD ["bin/rails", "server"]
  EXPOSE 3000
  ```

Some benefits of using a template with helpers are:

* Rails can update the helpers, and users can run `docker:render` to seamlessly pick up those changes.  For example, adding a new required apt package, or changing the recommended way to install Node and Yarn.

* Users can update their app, and run `docker:render` to incorporate relevant `Dockerfile` changes.  For example, adding Bootsnap and including `bootsnap precompile` commands, or adding Active Storage with the `image_processing` gem and including the `libvips` package.

* Users can update their system, and run `docker:render` to incorporate relevant `Dockerfile` changes.  For example, updating Ruby and
  matching the Ruby version, or migrating from Windows and dropping the binstub fixes.

* Third-party gems can extend `DockerfileHelpers` with new helpers or enhancements to existing helpers.  This may lessen pressure for Rails to support niche `Dockerfile` configurations out of the box.

The template and helpers in this commit also include a few improvements over the former default `Dockerfile`:

* Database apt packages are selected based on the database gems currently in use, reducing image size.  For example, going from `default-mysql-client libsqlite3-0 postgresql-client redis` to just `postgresql-client redis` reduces image size by 85MB.

* The `libvips` package is selected only if the app is currently using the `ruby-vips` gem.  For example, going from `libvips postgresql-client` to just `postgresql-client` reduces image size by 132MB.

* Build-time apt packages are installed on top of run-time packages to reduce downloads in the case of overlap (e.g. `lipvips` and all of its dependencies).

* Installation of apt packages and gems now uses persistent caches to reduce downloads when those layers are rebuilt.

* Precompiling assets now uses a persistent cache to speed up recompilation and to exclude the cache files from the final image.

* Fixes #47415.

* Fixes #47417.  More specifically, this pairs a preview version of Ruby (e.g. Ruby 3.2.0.preview1) with the appropriate Docker base image (e.g. `ruby:3.2.0-preview1-slim`).

---

TODO:
- [ ] Document `DockerfileHelpers`.
- [x] Add tests for `DockerfileHelpers`.
- [x] Add tests for `bin/rails docker:render`.

In a follow-up PR, I would like to possibly add a `bin/rails docker:build` command that automatically calls `bin/rails docker:render` before shelling out to `docker build`.
pr_comments: Sam Ruby is working on something even more comprehensive in https://github.com/rubys/dockerfile-rails. Will want to review that in depth first.

> Sam Ruby is working on something even more comprehensive in https://github.com/rubys/dockerfile-rails. Will want to review that in depth first.

Indeed!  But the approach taken in `rubys/dockerfile-rails` is to generate the `Dockerfile` from a set of options.  Each time the user wants to change an option, they re-generate the `Dockerfile`.  That means that any manual customizations they made to the `Dockerfile` (e.g. customizations not covered by the available options) will be overwritten.

With the approach in this PR, the user *is* intended to customize `config/Dockerfile.erb`, and then render the `Dockerfile` to reflect those changes.

Eventually, I would like the helpers in `DockerfileHelpers` to support many of the options from `rubys/dockerfile-rails`, but I wanted to get the basic structure in place first.

Going through the [options supported by `rubys/dockerfile-rails`](https://github.com/rubys/dockerfile-rails/blob/3e2ccdba22ae4230e3f44b5962f942d8841590a4/lib/generators/dockerfile_generator.rb#L64-L158):

* `ci` — "include test gems in bundle"

  This option [affects `BUNDLE_WITHOUT`](https://github.com/rubys/dockerfile-rails/blob/3e2ccdba22ae4230e3f44b5962f942d8841590a4/lib/generators/dockerfile_generator.rb#L441) and [install a few extra gems](https://github.com/rubys/dockerfile-rails/blob/3e2ccdba22ae4230e3f44b5962f942d8841590a4/lib/generators/templates/Dockerfile.erb#L37).

  For the former, users can modify the helper arguments in their template:

    ```erb
    FROM buildtime_packages as gems

    WORKDIR staged
    COPY Gemfile Gemfile.lock .
    # Change:
    <%= install_gems without: ["development"] %>
    # to:
    <%= install_gems without: ["development", "test"] %>
    ```

  For the latter, users can add `RUN gem install ...` to their template.

  If we want more turn-key support, I can investigate alternatives.

* `precompile` — "if set to "defer", assets:precompile will be done at deploy time"

  This involves modifying `bin/docker-entrypoint` among other things, so I think it is out of scope for this PR.  But I have an idea for a follow-up PR if we want to support this behavior.

* `bin-cd` — "modify binstubs to set working directory"

  I'm unclear on the purpose / benefit of this option.  But if we want to support it, I can add it as an option to `bin/rails binstubs:change` (see #47248).

* `cache` — "use build cache to speed up installs"

  This behavior is implemented by default in this PR.

* `prepare` — "include db:prepare step"

  To skip `db:prepare`, users can simply remove `ENTRYPOINT` from their template.

* `parallel` — "use build stages to install gems and node modules in parallel"

  This behavior is implemented by default in this PR.

* `swap` — "allocate swapspace"

  Similar to the `precompile` option, this involves modifying `bin/docker-entrypoint`, so I think it is out of scope for this PR.  But I can address it in a follow-up PR if we want to support this behavior.

* `compose` — "generate a docker-compose.yml file"

  Out of scope for this PR.

* `redis` / `sqlite3` / `postgresql` / `mysql` — include the relevant database packages

  The `runtime_db_packages` and `buildtime_db_packages` helpers in this PR support options to include / exclude the various database packages.  Currently, all default to being included (just like in `main`), but I would like to tackle auto-selection in a follow-up PR.

* `platform` — "image platform (example: linux/arm64)"

  Users can simply add `--platform` to thier template, e.g.:

    ```erb
    FROM --platform=linux/arm64 ruby:<%= ruby_version %>-slim as initial
    ```

* `jemalloc` — "use jemalloc alternative malloc implementation"

  I have not tested this, but according to [Fly's own documentation](https://github.com/superfly/docs/blob/13b11c74b5254cac74cef4f78ce1cfa2a533047b/rails/cookbooks/deploy.html.md.erb#L22-L28), jemalloc only requires the following:

    ```dockerfile
    RUN apt-get install libjemalloc2
    ENV LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libjemalloc.so.2
    ENV MALLOC_CONF=dirty_decay_ms:1000,narenas:2,background_thread:true
    ```

  So users can simply add those lines to their template.  It would also be easy to add a helper for those lines, if we desire.  Notably, the `rubys/dockerfile-rails` `jemalloc` option is boolean and doesn't support tweaking `MALLOC_CONF`, whereas an editable template does.

* `fullstaq` — "use Fullstaq Ruby image from Quay.io"

  I believe the only purpose for this option [was to support YJIT](https://github.com/superfly/docs/blob/13b11c74b5254cac74cef4f78ce1cfa2a533047b/rails/cookbooks/deploy.html.md.erb#L38-L44).  However, YJIT is now supported in the `ruby:3.2.0-slim` image (see docker-library/ruby#400), so I believe this option is no longer a concern.

* `yjit` — "enable YJIT optimizing compiler"

  YJIT is supported out-of-the-box in the latest `ruby:3.2.0-slim` image, and users can set `RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1` to enable it.  This PR includes `# ENV RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1` in the default template so users can simply uncomment that line in their template.

* `label` — "Add Docker label(s)"

  Users can simply add `LABEL` statements to their template.

* `nginx` — "Serve static files with nginx"

  This generates an NGINX config file, but it is [inlined in the Dockerfile](https://github.com/rubys/dockerfile-rails/blob/3e2ccdba22ae4230e3f44b5962f942d8841590a4/lib/generators/templates/_nginx.erb#L6-L31).  I'm not sure if this is something we want to support, but it would be possible to add a helper for it.  In either case, I think it is out of scope for this PR.

* `root` — "Run application as root user"

  Since #47192, the generated `Dockerfile` adds an application user, and that is carried over into this PR.  To run as root, users can remove the `RUN useradd` and `USER` statements from their template.  (And optionally remove `--chown=1000`, but the root user's access shouldn't be affected either way.)

* `add-base` / `add-build` / `add-deploy` / `remove-base` / `remove-build` / `remove-deploy` — add / remove packages to install for the build / deploy stages

  Users can add or remove packages from the default lists by modifying the helper arguments in their template:

    ```erb
    FROM initial as runtime_packages

    <%= install_packages runtime_packages + %w[add] - %w[remove], skip_recommends: true %>


    FROM runtime_packages as buildtime_packages

    <%= install_packages buildtime_packages + %w[add] - %w[remove] %>
    ```

* `env-base` / `env-build` / `env-deploy` — additional environment variables to set for build / deploy stages

  Users can simply add `ENV` statements to their template.

* `arg-base` / `arg-build` / `arg-deploy` — additional build arguments for build / deploy stages

  Users can simply add `ARG` statements to their template.

The more I've been working with apps on our end that use the current default Dockerfile as the base, the less I'm inclined to think we should add too much chrome around it. The Dockerfile is in many cases more than a build artifact. It's a configuration you tweak and keep alive. I don't think there's enough value here to have an automated system keep that file somehow automatically current. We're better off teaching people how they migrate the base with the actual Dockerfile than to wrap all of that in a heavy abstract/cli interface.

In terms of the specific changes, I also find that the extra stages make things harder to follow for a pretty negligible win. 

The biggest win in terms of performance is likely the bundle cache. It's just such a wart. I'd rather try to see if we can't upstream a docker cache-friendly setup for bundler before including multiple lines of arcane configuration.

I've reworked how the runtime and buildtime apt packages are derived.  Now installed packages are based on which gems will be loaded for the targeted gem groups.  This simplifies several of the helpers, and it eliminates unnecessary packages for no extra code cost.

For example, if an application is only using the `pg` and `redis` gems, the apt packages for MySQL and SQLite will not be installed.  Going from `default-mysql-client libsqlite3-0 postgresql-client redis` to just `postgresql-client redis` reduces image size by 85MB.

Similarly, the `libvips` package is installed only if the application is currently using the `ruby-vips` gem.  Going from `libvips postgresql-client` to just `postgresql-client`, for example, reduces image size by 132MB.

---

@dhh

> The Dockerfile is in many cases more than a build artifact. It's a configuration you tweak and keep alive.

> The biggest win in terms of performance is likely the bundle cache. It's just such a wart.

I think you and I are in agreement in terms of tweaking the Dockerfile and avoiding warts.  In fact, that was the motivation behind this PR.  I wanted a file that I could tweak freely (not a file that would be overwritten by a generator a la `rubys/dockerfile-rails`), and I wanted it to be optimized but still look clean.

The workflow I envision is that users would edit `config/Dockerfile.erb` directly, and it would never be overwritten by a generator or `app:update`.  The helpers keep the template readable, without missing out on build optimizations.  The helpers can also reduce image size by excluding unnecessary apt packages, without adding extra steps in the future if the application needs those packages (e.g. after `db:system:change` or adding a gem).

> In terms of the specific changes, I also find that the extra stages make things harder to follow for a pretty negligible win.

I don't have strong feelings about that.  I assumed (based on prior discussions) that build parallelism was a goal, and thought that perhaps the extra stages might improve readability in the same way as breaking up a large Ruby method into smaller methods.

The commit I just pushed goes back to only three stages.  It also evaluates the Node conditional at app generation time.  Meaning applications that don't use Node will not have the `if node?` code in their `config/Dockerfile.erb`.  If they switch to using Node, they will have to add the missing code, but the helpers make it short and sweet, so it seems like a reasonable trade-off.  Here is what the user-editable `config/Dockerfile.erb` will look like in that case:

```erb
<%#
Run `bin/rails docker:render` to render this template to a Dockerfile in your
application's root directory. For more information about the helpers used in
this template, see https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/Rails/DockerfileHelpers.html
-%>

# Base image for multi-stage build.
FROM ruby:<%= ruby_version %>-slim as base

ENV BUNDLE_APP_CONFIG=.bundle
# ENV RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1

<%= install_packages runtime_packages, skip_recommends: true %>


# Throw-away build stage to reduce size of final image.
FROM base as build

<%= install_packages buildtime_packages %>

WORKDIR /build

COPY Gemfile Gemfile.lock* .
<%= install_gems %>


# Final stage for application image.
FROM base

RUN useradd rails
USER 1000

WORKDIR /rails

COPY --chown=1000 --from=build /build .
COPY --chown=1000 . .

<%= prepare_app %>

ENTRYPOINT ["bin/docker-entrypoint"]
CMD ["bin/rails", "server"]
EXPOSE 3000
```

> It's a configuration you tweak and keep alive.

I will assert that the typical Rails developer doesn't have your background.  I've written more on that here: https://github.com/rubys/dockerfile-rails/blob/main/MOTIVATION.md

Having deployed this for less than a month, it already has significantly reduced the amount of time I am spending supporting Rails developers.

In any case, I am working on dockerfile-rails because *I* need it.  Everybody is welcome to either make use of it directly or steal the pieces they need.

I respect the approach both of you are taking, and I think there are definitely situations where they can make sense. But as a default, I'd like to see us stick to a single Dockerfile generated at "rails new" time. It should weigh the trade-off between optimization and clarity, but lean towards clarity over optimization. I think we're close.

In terms of the libvips/db dependencies, I think we can leave them in as is, but add a small note for someone to remove what they don't need. Out of the box, the Dockerfile should Just Work, with no alteration, no reiteration, regardless of which db you pick, and whether you use libvips or not. Then make it easy for someone to snip out the bits they don't need to save a little extra weight.

@rubys

> > It's a configuration you tweak and keep alive.
>
> I will assert that the typical Rails developer doesn't have your background. I've written more on that here: https://github.com/rubys/dockerfile-rails/blob/main/MOTIVATION.md
>
> Having deployed this for less than a month, it already has significantly reduced the amount of time I am spending supporting Rails developers.

Is there a difficulty / expertise threshold where users could reasonably be expected to make direct edits to a `Dockerfile`?  For example, would it be reasonable to expect that a user can add an `ENV` statement to a `Dockerfile`?

If there is such a threshold, do you have an idea of where it might lie for typical Rails developers?  Do you have particular sticking points in mind?

The target here is that the default Dockerfile will get your hello world app deployed without alteration. If you start adding dependencies that force updates to the Dockerfile, we can help you with documentation. 

But I don't want to wrap the Dockerfile in another generating abstraction. Totally fine for such abstractions to exist as external gems, of course. Just won't be the default in Rails.

Some background on my perspective.  Deploying a fly.io application starts with a dockerfile.  If you don't have one, we will provide one for you.  The one we provided before I joined roughly looked like the one rails 7.1 will produce for a jsbundling application.  One of the first things I did is to replace the static dockerfile we provided with a template so that import map applications will see a smaller Dockerfile.

And, yes, we accompanied this with documentation.

If you go to https://community.fly.io/ , click on the search icon in the top right, enter "rails" and press enter and click on a random post you can see the result.

A few of my favorites:
  * One person found a post indicating how to copy files from an alpine image.  Ruby images are debian.  libc is different so any attempt to make use of the library they copied resulted in a SEGV.
  * One person found a post indicating what Debian libraries that they needed.  So they added them.  This got the build state to work, but then they failed at deploy.  I had to point out what the FROM statements, and most importantly what the comments immediately before those FROM statements, said.  This was this month, so the dockerfiles fly.io produce closely match the ones in the current Rails 7.1 template.  Adding libraries to the throwaway build step won't make it to deployment.
  * One person saw a failure and realized that a library needed to be added.  You can 'ssh' into fly machines, so that's what he did.  He installed the library, and then reran deploy.  That produced a new machine, and didn't fix his error.  This example is my favorite as rerunning `bin/rails generate dockerfile` fixed his problem the right way.

To be clear, each of these people were intelligent, and searched out solutions.

I've been involved with bringing new people to Ruby on Rails for many years, and can confidently state that's not the experience a Rails developer expects. 

So, think of my input as being from your future.  Been there, done that.  People generally don't like their first deploy experience to be a research project.  The current Rails 7.1 approach will increase support costs for everyone.  I've only deployed this new approach for a few weeks so far, and the number of rails support questions has dropped dramatically.  And if I'm reading my metrics correctly, we are seeing approximately 100 new rails users a day, 7 days a week.  And best of all, once I get a new problem, I can generally find a way to fix it for future developers with similar configurations.

But you guys do what you want.  Expect to be mocked mercilessly and for satisfaction with Rails to decrease.  Hopefully word of mouth will help people find the dockerfile-rails gem

Appreciate your perspective. I fail to see how going from "no default Dockerfile, you're on your own" to "great default Dockerfile" from Rails 7 to 7.1 will somehow trigger Rails to be "mocked mercilessly"(??) or satisfaction to decrease. But hey, happy you found something that works for your business, and that's great. Lots of respect for Fly.

I'm going to close this out for now, though. @jonathanhefner, we can work on bringing the other improvements into the default Dockerfile in another set of tickets. Thanks again for working on this!

For anyone interested, I have extracted many of the ideas in this PR into a gem named [`dockhand`](https://github.com/jonathanhefner/dockhand).  But, instead of having to render a `Dockerfile` template, `dockhand` runs *inside* the container when building an image.  For example:

  ```dockerfile
  COPY Gemfile Gemfile.lock .
  RUN gem install dockhand \
   && dockhand install-packages --gem-runtime --clean
  ```

will install the apt packages needed at runtime by common gems in the `Gemfile`, such as `libsqlite3-0` if using the `sqlite3` gem or `postgresql-client` if using the `pg` gem.

Or, for example:

  ```dockerfile
  COPY package.json* .node-version* .
  RUN dockhand install-node --optional
  ```

will install the correct version of Node.js *if* the application has a `.node-version` file or a `package.json` file with an `engines.node` value.  (If the application has a `package.json` file but no Node.js version, the build will raise a [helpful error](https://github.com/jonathanhefner/dockhand/blob/v0.1.0/lib/dockhand/command.rb#L91-L97).)

*Taking things a step further,* I've been working on [`railbarge`](https://github.com/jonathanhefner/railbarge), which is a set of Docker base images that use `dockhand` with `ONBUILD` instructions.  The goal of `railbarge` is to provide a turn-key `Dockerfile` UX suitable for most Rails apps.

For example, the following `Dockerfile`:

  ```dockerfile
  ARG RUBY_VERSION=3.2.1

  FROM railbarge/builder:ruby-$RUBY_VERSION as builder

  FROM railbarge/app:ruby-$RUBY_VERSION
  COPY --from=builder /artifacts /
  ```

will work for a Rails 7.0 app out of the box:

  ```console
  $ rails -v
  Rails 7.0.4.2

  $ rails new my_cool_app && cd my_cool_app

  $ bin/rails g scaffold post title:string

  $ cat << 'DOCKERFILE' > Dockerfile
  FROM railbarge/builder:ruby-3.2.1 as builder
  FROM railbarge/app:ruby-3.2.1
  COPY --from=builder /artifacts /
  DOCKERFILE

  $ echo '/config/master.key' >> .dockerignore

  $ docker build -t my_cool_app .

  $ docker run -p 3000:3000 -e RAILS_MASTER_KEY=$(cat config/master.key) --rm my_cool_app &
  ...
  == 20230307202849 CreatePosts: migrating ======================================
  -- create_table(:posts)
     -> 0.0011s
  == 20230307202849 CreatePosts: migrated (0.0011s) =============================

  => Booting Puma
  ...
  * Listening on http://0.0.0.0:3000
  Use Ctrl-C to stop

  $ curl --head http://0.0.0.0:3000/posts
  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  ...

  $ fg 1
  $ ^C
  ```

It will also work with `jsbundling-rails` if provided a Node.js version (such as with `node --version > .node-version`).

`railbarge` can also accomodate more sophisticated setups with only small changes to the `Dockerfile`.  I've written about a few more use cases in https://discuss.rubyonrails.org/t/rails-dockerfile-futures/82091/37.

Feedback is welcome! :smiley:

issue_context.title: Change from Gem.ruby_version to RUBY_VERSION
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce

Run `rails new` with any Ruby with a gem patch level

### Expected behavior

Dockerfile contains FROM statement specifying a three part version number for the Ruby image

### Actual behavior

Dockerfile contains FROM statement specifying a non-existent ruby image containing four parts

### System configuration
**Rails version**: 7.1

**Ruby version**: any ruby version with a patch level

## See also

https://github.com/rubys/dockerfile-rails/commit/57e066da24b86d038bb862f5300c5c747e47309e
comments: :thinking: Patch level was removed with Ruby 3.0 if I remember well (did some checks locally and it seems to). Ruby 2.7 is EOL soon. It would be also possible to fix this by removing Ruby 2.7 support (seems to EOL at 31.3.2023). But maybe that's too drastic.

An actual fly.io user with Ruby 3.1.0.0 failed to deploy due to this error.  See https://community.fly.io/t/rails-cant-deploy-an-app-following-the-getting-started-guide/10026/4?u=rubys where the error was reported.
You're right, it seems as a problem in actual RubyGems. Using `RUBY_VERSION` makes better sense then.

> See https://community.fly.io/t/rails-cant-deploy-an-app-following-the-getting-started-guide/10026/4?u=rubys where the error was reported.

I read through this thread and it looks like the user was using Rails 7.0.4. Perhaps their rubygems version is not up to date? (Ruby 3.1.2 shipped with rubygems 3.3.7)

The change to `Gem.ruby_version` from `RUBY_VERSION` was discussed previously in #45979. The conclusion was that for Rails 7.1, the minimum required rubygems version would be bumped in #46817 because previous versions returned extra decimals as you describe.

So as long as the `Gem.ruby_version` usage is only on the main branch and not on `7-0-stable`, I think it is preferable over `RUBY_VERSION`.

> So as long as the Gem.ruby_version usage is only on the main branch and not on 7-0-stable, I think it is preferable over RUBY_VERSION.

Just curious, why?

I have a business need to support prior versions of Rails; given this, what am I missing out since I'm currently using RUBY_VERSION?

> Just curious, why?
> 
> I have a business need to support prior versions of Rails; given this, what am I missing out since I'm currently using RUBY_VERSION?

The benefit would be being able to generate Dockerfiles pointing to prerelease versions of Ruby, as described in #45979 but in this case for the Dockerfile instead of the Gemfile.

I suppose that would also require a small change because `Gem.ruby_version` would generate `3.2.0.preview3` but the image tags use a dash instead :/

https://hub.docker.com/layers/library/ruby/3.2.0-preview3/images/sha256-a4a644a3675101fb543a966450769257d7f40cd4112ecb3e3c67f189c695b4cf

---

I was assuming this issue was about updating this line, so that's why I was only thinking about Rails 7.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/6cea2589a45a67a3e58cddc2d5d223f92c57fb76/railties/lib/rails/generators/rails/app/templates/Dockerfile.tt#L4

Maybe I'm not understanding what the plan is to support older Rails versions. Is the goal to use `dockerfile-rails`? In that case you could raise the minimum required rubygems version to `">= 3.3.13"` and `Gem.ruby_version` should work as expected.

Unrelated to the current discussion, are these issues you've opened TODO items for yourself that you plan to open PRs for? Or are they open issues that you wouldn't mind someone else grabbing?

> prerelease versions of Ruby

gotcha.  Thanks.  modulo that small bug, I can see the value.  It is not a use case that I'm likely to encounter, but given that future Rails 7.1 apps will have upgraded rubygems, any Dockerfiles generated with the current template will work with fly.io, so this issue can be closed.

> Is the goal to use dockerfile-rails? 

That's a multi-faceted question :-)

I believe that there is significant overlap between the requirements that Rails, fly.io, and others like mrsk have, and would love to collaborate.  If, for example, you personally were to create a substantive PR on dockerfile-rails, my response likely would be to add you as a collaborator.

Overlap doesn't mean congruence.  For example, I have customers running Rails 5 apps on unsupported versions of Ruby.  Yes, they should upgrade, but it isn't my best interest to make that a barrier or prerequisite.

But, yes, is is my stated preference that Rails 7.1 uses dockerfile-rails much in the same way that it runs commands like `bin/rails turbo:install stimulus:install` during the creation of a new application.

> issues that you wouldn't mind someone else grabbing

The current batch are issues that actual fly.io customers have encountered that I thought (in this case mistakenly) that would prevent future Rails 7.1 applications from being immediately deployable on fly.io.

And ones that I hope that somebody would pick up.  I have an unpublished cathartic rant regarding my experience with the current process for pull requests for Rals 7.1.
